reference_title: California Trenching and Shoring Manual (Caltrans, June 2011, Revision 2 - July 2025)

sections.title: Soil Identification, Classification, Description, and Presentation
sections.summary: Soil for shoring design is classified from the Geotechnical Design Report / Foundation Report and Log of Test Borings (LOTB), or by a competent person per Cal/OSHA CSO 1541.1 Appendix A (Stable Rock, Type A, B, or C). Group name/symbol follow ASTM D2488 (visual-manual) or D2487 (USCS lab). Soils are coarse-grained (>50% retained on the No. 200 sieve: gravel G, sand S) or fine-grained (>50% passing: silt M, clay C, organic O), further graded W/P or by plasticity L/H.
sections.body: The Contractor can obtain soil classification from the Geotechnical Design Report or Foundation Report and corresponding Log of Test Borings (LOTB), by independent sampling and analysis, or by having a competent person classify the soil per Cal/OSHA Construction Safety Orders, Section 1541.1, Appendix A, Soil Classification. The Cal/OSHA methods use at least one visual and one manual analysis to classify the soil as stable rock, Type A, Type B, or Type C; each type is assigned an unconfined compressive strength. The descriptive sequence is a group name and group symbol (e.g. 'SANDY lean CLAY (CL)') from ASTM D2488 (visual-manual, if no lab testing) or ASTM D2487 (USCS, if lab particle-size and plasticity tests are done), followed by density/consistency, color, moisture, etc. Coarse-grained soils retain more than 50 percent on/above the No. 200 sieve (0.075 mm); GRAVEL (G) and SAND (S) are graded well-graded (W) or poorly graded (P), with silt (M) or clay (C) content (e.g. SW, SM). Fine-grained soils pass more than 50 percent through the No. 200 sieve; SILT (M), CLAY (C), ORGANIC (O) are low (L) or high (H) plasticity (e.g. CL, ML).
key_points: Cal/OSHA classifies soils as Stable Rock, Type A, Type B, or Type C (CSO 1541.1 App A)
Group name/symbol from ASTM D2488 (visual-manual) or D2487 (USCS, lab)
Coarse-grained: >50% retained on No. 200 sieve (gravel G, sand S; W/P, M/C content)
Fine-grained: >50% passing No. 200 sieve (silt M, clay C, organic O; L/H plasticity)
It is the Engineer's responsibility to verify the soil properties used in the Contractor's shoring submittal
sections.applicability: Establishing the soil classification underlying a shoring design or review

sections.title: Standard Penetration Test (SPT) and Granular Soil Properties
sections.summary: The SPT N value (blows/ft for the split-spoon over 12 in.) is energy-corrected to N60. Table 3-1 correlates N60 to apparent density, friction angle phi, and unit weight (moist/submerged) for granular soils. Table 3-2 (Caltrans 'simplified typical soil values') lists phi, gamma, Ka, and equivalent fluid weight Kw = Ka*gamma by soil class and density; use gamma >= 115 pcf minimum for active pressure when data is insufficient. The Department does NOT use SPT to estimate cohesive shear strength.
sections.body: The Standard Penetration Test (SPT) obtains a disturbed sample; the number of hammer blows to drive the split-spoon 12 inches is the N value, corrected to N60 for hammer energy efficiency. Table 3-1, Properties of Granular Soils, relates N60 to apparent density (Very Loose / Loose / Medium Dense / Dense / Very Dense), relative density (%), friction angle phi (deg), and unit weight (pcf, moist and submerged). Note the LOTB and boring records report the field N value, not N60. Table 3-2, Simplified Typical Soil Values, prepared by Geotechnical Services for average trench conditions, lists phi, gamma, the active coefficient Ka, and the equivalent fluid weight Kw = Ka*gamma (pcf, also called EFP) by soil class (gravel/coarse sand, medium sand, fine sand, silty sand/sandy silt, silt) and density (dense/medium dense/loose). For active pressure use a unit weight of gamma = 115 pcf minimum when insufficient soils data is known. It is not the Department's practice to use the SPT to estimate the shear strength of cohesive soil; field tests (pocket penetrometer, Torvane) and lab tests (triaxial, unconfined compression, direct shear) are more accurate (Table 3-3 for cohesive consistency vs unconfined compressive strength).
key_points: N value (field) is energy-corrected to N60 before using Table 3-1
Table 3-1: granular density / phi / unit weight vs N60
Table 3-2: phi, gamma, Ka, and equivalent fluid weight Kw = Ka*gamma by soil class and density
Use gamma >= 115 pcf minimum for active pressure when soils data is insufficient
SPT is NOT used to estimate cohesive shear strength; use field/lab tests (Table 3-3)

sections.title: Field and Laboratory Tests; Test Reliability
sections.summary: Not all methods of evaluating soil shear strength are equally accurate, so the source of the strength data must be considered when evaluating a proposed trenching or shoring system. Table 3-4 rates SPT, CPT, pocket penetrometer, Torvane, vane shear, triaxial, unconfined compression and direct shear for coarse- vs fine-grained soil. The pocket penetrometer gives cohesive qu (tsf); the Torvane gives Su and is an acceptable Cal/OSHA manual test. Field tests need to be used with all the materials information in the logs and reports. Where a cohesion value c is used, three conditions are recommended to be addressed with each shoring submittal.
sections.body: Not all methods of evaluating soil shear strength are equally accurate. Therefore, the source of the shear strength data must be considered when evaluating a proposed trenching or shoring system. Table 3-4 lists field and laboratory tests used to measure or estimate soil shear strength and an indication of their reliability (coarse-grained / fine-grained soil): Standard Penetration Test (SPT, ASTM D1586) Good / Poor; Cone Penetration Test (CPT, ASTM D3441) Good / Fair; Pocket Penetrometer Not applicable / Fair; Torvane (shearvane) Not applicable / Fair; Vane Shear (ASTM D2573) Not applicable / Very good; Triaxial Compression (UU, CU; ASTM D2850) Very good* / Very good; Unconfined Compression (ASTM D2166) Not applicable / Very good; Direct Shear (ASTM D3080) Good* / Fair (*recovery of undisturbed samples can be difficult). The Torvane and pocket penetrometer tests are field tests that may be noted on the LOTB; the Department uses them to aid in determining the uniformity of the cohesive soil encountered. The Contractor may perform their own tests while excavating and may overly emphasize these field tests, but the tests need to be used in conjunction with all the materials information in the logs and geotechnical reports. The pocket penetrometer provides a value for a cohesive soil's unconfined compressive strength, qu, in tons per square foot; the Torvane (or shearvane) determines cohesive soils' undrained shear strength (Su). Use of a Torvane is an acceptable practice under Cal/OSHA CSO 1541.1 Appendix A, subsection (d)(2)(D); where the Contractor proposes a Torvane, consult the SC Falsework Engineer in Structure Construction Headquarters. For projects utilizing a cohesion value, c, it is recommended the following conditions be included and addressed with each shoring submittal: (1) methods used to prevent tension cracks from developing at the top of the excavation; (2) methods used to prevent water from ponding at the top of and the toe of the slope; (3) verification that the soil is consistent and homogeneous throughout the excavation (p. 3-10). (Section 3-8, Contractor Soil Investigations, p. 3-11, which the stored text holds no section for, lists the factors the Engineer will consider when assigning strength parameters: the method by which the shear strength was determined (Table 3-4), the variability of the subsurface profile, and the number and distribution of shear strength tests; it also says soil test results need to be used with caution, since laboratory reports may or may not include safety factors in the reported results.)

Pocket penetrometer -> cohesive unconfined compressive strength qu (tsf)
Torvane (shearvane) -> undrained shear strength Su (Cal/OSHA-acceptable manual test)
Table 3-4 rates vane shear, triaxial and unconfined compression Very good for fine-grained soil
Where c is used, address with each submittal: preventing tension cracks at the top, preventing ponding at the top and toe, and verifying the soil is consistent and homogeneous (p. 3-10)
Field tests (Torvane, pocket penetrometer) need to be used in conjunction with all the materials information in the logs and geotechnical reports

sections.title: Shear Strength
sections.summary: Soil shear strength is measured by the friction angle phi and the cohesion c. One of the fundamental relationships governing it is tau_f = c + sigma*tan(phi) (Eq. 3-7-1; Mohr-Coulomb criteria, Figure 3-3); the strength envelope is in general a curve tangent to the Mohr circles. In fine-grained (cohesive) soils, strength is initially insensitive to confining pressure and the criterion simplifies to tau_f = Su (Eq. 3-7-2), Su the undrained shear strength. A fine-grained soil unloaded by excavation expands and has the potential to lose shear strength over time.
sections.body: The shear strength of soil is measured by two parameters, the angle of internal friction phi (the resistance to interparticle slip) and the soil cohesion (the interparticle attraction of the soil particles). The design of most geotechnical structures requires a quantitative determination of the soil shear strength. One of the fundamental relationships governing soil shear strength is tau_f = c + sigma*tan(phi) (Eq. 3-7-1), where tau_f = soil shear strength at failure, phi = internal friction angle, sigma = normal stress, c = soil cohesion (Figure 3-3, Mohr-Coulomb Criteria). In general, the relationship between shear strength and normal stress is not linear for large stress ranges; the strength envelope is a curve tangent to the Mohr circles, and the point of tangency represents the stress conditions on the failure plane of the sample. In fine-grained (cohesive) soils, shear strength is initially insensitive to confining pressure since the strength is derived through cohesion; for cohesive soils the failure criterion simplifies to tau_f = Su (Eq. 3-7-2), where Su is the undrained shear strength. Cohesive soils will consolidate or swell over time depending on whether the soil has been loaded or unloaded, respectively. Trenching and shoring work often reduces soil loading, as in an excavation; a fine-grained soil subjected to unloading will then expand and has the potential to lose shear strength over time.
key_points: Mohr-Coulomb: tau_f = c + sigma*tan(phi) (Eq. 3-7-1)
Undrained cohesive soil: tau_f = Su (Eq. 3-7-2)
A fine-grained soil unloaded by excavation expands and has the potential to lose shear strength over time
The strength-normal stress relationship is in general not linear for large stress ranges; the envelope is a curve tangent to the Mohr circles

equations.description: Mohr-Coulomb shear strength at failure: tau_f = c + sigma*tan(phi).
Cohesive soils: the failure criterion simplifies to tau_f = Su, Su the undrained shear strength.

sections.applicability: Defining the shear strength parameters (c, phi, Su) used in shoring and slope analyses

sections.title: Special Ground Conditions
sections.summary: Some excavations encounter soil/rock needing special consideration: fractured rock (toppling/wedge failure on adverse bedding), organic soil/peat (compressible, decomposes), clay and shale (crack/spall/swell/slake on exposure, weaken when unloaded), running soil (no shear strength, flows; c = 0), and quick conditions (upward seepage suspends grains; stabilize by equalizing water levels). The geotechnical report typically identifies these; contact Geotechnical Services.
sections.body: Occasionally excavations are made into soil or rock with properties that require special consideration in the design of the shoring system; the special condition must be defined and the expected behavior of the material during and after excavation and installation must be understood. Typically the geotechnical report identifies these conditions, and it is recommended that Geotechnical Services be contacted for assistance. Examples: (1) Fractured rock - adversely oriented bedding or fracturing, which would allow toppling or wedge failure into the excavation, should be identified and accounted for in the design of the shoring system. (2) Organic soil (peat) - compressible and subject to decomposition causing volume change. (3) Clay and shale - subject to cracking/spalling on exposure to air, swelling/slaking when exposed to water, and weakening when unloaded; excavating such materials might require protection of the shoring system to help retain natural moisture content; design analyses need to account for the expected disturbed strength of the retained material, which might be weaker than in-situ. (4) Running soil - cannot stand even short term, little shear strength, flows with virtually no angle of repose; cohesion c = 0. (5) Quick condition - upward water flow makes the soil buoyant and suspends the grains; can occur in silts and sands, best stabilized by equalizing water levels (see Section 10-4, Piping).
key_points: Fractured rock: adverse bedding/fracturing allowing toppling or wedge failure should be identified and accounted for
Organic soil/peat: compressible, decomposes, large volume change
Clay/shale: crack/spall/swell/slake on exposure; design for disturbed (weaker) strength
Running soil: little shear strength, flows; cohesion c = 0
Quick condition: upward seepage suspends grains; equalize water levels (see piping, Ch 10-4)
sections.applicability: Flagging special soil/rock conditions that alter shoring design assumptions
